blocks.text: Now if I wished to add everything that Alkazuinius, Ibnolbatrik, Avicenna, Serapion, Sariph, Abenbitar, Alcamus and other Arabs say about the medicinal virtues of this bird, the matter would grow beyond measure. It will therefore suffice for us to add a few things out of many, from which it may be clear what bird the Arabs call by this name. 1. The dung of the rachama expels the embryo. Alkazuinius: ذرقها ان احتملته المراة القت جنينها [dharquhā in iḥtamalathu al-marʾa alqat janīnahā], If a woman applies its dung, she expels the embryo. Avicenna: قيل ان زبله يسقط الجنين تبخيرا [qīla inna zibluhu yusqiṭu al-janīn tabkhīran], Its dung is said to expel the embryo by fumigation. Behold, the same is found in Dioscorides concerning the dung of the vulture, in the chapter On dung in book 2: Γυπὸς ἄφοδος ὑποθυμιαθεῖσα ἔμβρυα ἐκτινάσσειν παραδέδοται [gypos aphodos hypothymiatheisa embrya ektinassein paradedotai], Vulture's dung, used as a fumigation, is said to drive out the foetus. And in Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 34:
Moreover, they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, [col. 306] so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close.

2. The feather of the rachama also assists childbirth. Sariph: وان اخذت ريشه من جناحها اليمن ووضعت بين رجلي المطلغة سهل اولادها [wa-in ukhidhat rīsha min janāḥihā al-yumn wa-wuḍiʿat bayna rijlay al-muṭlagha sahhala awlādahā], When a feather is taken from its right wing and placed at the feet of a woman in labour, it relieves the pains of childbirth. So also Alcamus under رخم [rakham] racham. Pliny says the same of the vulture's feather, book 29, chapter 4: A vulture's feather placed under the feet assists women in labour. And Sextus, book 2, chapter 2: It makes them give birth without labour. [III, 59] 3. The gall of the rachama cures albugo [white opacity of the eye]. Alkazuinius: يكتحل بمرارتها وحدها لبياض العين [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā waḥdahā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn], From the vulture's gall alone an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eye. Avicenna: يكتحل بمرارتها لبياض العين بالما البارد [yuktaḥalu bi-marāratihā li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn bi-l-mā al-bārid], From its gall with cold water an eye-salve is made for albugo of the eyes. The vulture's gall has the same power. Pliny, book 29, chapter 6, after saying that eagle's gall is applied as an ointment for clouding, dimness and cataracts of the eyes: The same power is also in vulture's gall, etc. Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 14:

If sluggish old age draws darkness over the eyes, drops pressed from fennel with flowing honey have been able to wipe away the ill, or the gall of the black vulture, if blades of celandine are mixed with it.

Marcellus: Combine a scruple of the gall of a cock, or of a vulture, which is far more beneficial, with an ounce of the best honey, well ground, keep it in a copper box, and use it for anointing when needed. Nothing relieves dimness more powerfully than this. Galen, Euporista, book 1, chapter 44: Vulture's gall, with juice of horehound and Attic honey, cures every dimness of the eyes and incipient cataract. Sextus: Vulture's gall, etc. dispels all dimness.

4. The liver of the rachama is useful for those possessed by a demon. Alcamus: كبده يشوي ويسحق ويسقي المجنون ثلثة ايام كل يوم ثلاث مرات ويبريه [kabiduhu yushwā wa-yusḥaqu wa-yusqā al-majnūn thalatha ayyām kull yawm thalāth marrāt wa-yubrīhi], Its liver, roasted and ground, is given to the demoniac to drink for three days, three times daily, and he recovers. So also Damir. And not much differently Abenbitar: كبدها شوي ويسحق ويداف بخل ويسقي من به جنون كل يوم ثلاث مرات ثلاثة ايام متواليه فيبريه [kabiduhā shuwiya wa-yusḥaqu wa-yudāfu bi-khall wa-yusqā man bihi junūn kull yawm thalāth marrāt thalātha ayyām mutawāliya fa-yubrīhi], Its liver is roasted, ground, and steeped in vinegar, and given to drink to one who is possessed by a demon, three times daily for three days, for three continuous days, and it heals him. Indeed, concerning epilepsy, in which there seems to be θεῖόν τι [theion ti], something divine, the older writers had handed down something similar. Pliny: Vulture's liver, drunk with its own blood for thrice seven days, is commended against epilepsy. So also Sextus and Aesculapius.

5. Here is another remedy from the flesh of the rachama! Sariph: لحم الرخم اذا خلط بخردل وجفف وبخر به المعقود عن النسا سبع [col. 307] مرات اطلقه ذلك [laḥm al-rakham idhā khuliṭa bi-khardal wa-juffifa wa-bukhkhira bihi al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā sabʿ marrāt aṭlaqahu dhālika], If the flesh of the rachama, mixed with mustard and dried, is used to fumigate a sufferer from sciatica [III, 60] seven times, he will be freed from his illness. Alcamus: التبخير بتجفيف لحمه مخلوطا بخردل سبع مرات يحل المعقود عن النسا [al-tabkhīr bi-tajfīf laḥmihi makhlūṭan bi-khardal sabʿ marrāt yaḥullu al-maʿqūd ʿan al-nasā], A fumigation from its dried flesh, mixed with mustard, repeated seven times, will heal one suffering from sciatica. But in both places, instead of خردل [khardal] chardal, that is, mustard, we think one should read حرمل [ḥarmal] charmal, that is, rue: because in Serenus Sammonicus, chapter 55, we find:
But if a hidden pain burns the sluggish sinews, apply the excised fat of a vulture, and rue, etc.
